explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Amos says, "Woe to those at ease in Zion and those secure on Mount Samaria…" (Amos 6:1). These folks have settled in so deep they've got dents in the couch. I think Amos picked those two words because comfort can get a little too comfortable.

Nope, the text paints the opposite picture. Amos calls them "at ease" and "secure." Nobody in this verse is peeking out the window or checking the locks. I'd say these folks are sleeping with the door wide open.

Not quite, friend. Verse 1 says "at ease" and "secure," which is the exact opposite of worn out. These are the distinguished ones of the foremost nation, and the house of Israel comes to them. Hungry people don't usually get described like that.

explanations.answer: Are you better than these kingdoms
explanations.explanation: Yes, and it's a pointed one. Amos asks, "Are you better than these kingdoms? Is their territory larger than yours?" (Amos 6:2). He sends them to Calneh, Hamath and Gath first, so they can look before they answer. I think that's a question you answer a little quieter than you ask it.

explanations.answer: Who rules over these kingdoms now
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a fine question, but it's not what Amos asks. He asks, "Are you better than these kingdoms?" He's comparing Israel's leaders to those places, and he never asks about who sits on their thrones. I'd say he's pointing the finger right back at them.

explanations.answer: Will you trade with these kingdoms
explanations.explanation: Close to a business meeting, but no. Amos doesn't talk about trade at all. After the tour he asks, "Are you better than these kingdoms?" Then he adds, "Is their territory larger than yours?" (Amos 6:2).

Careful, this one has a twist. Amos says, "You dismiss the day of calamity and bring near a reign of violence." The reign of violence isn't pushed away, it gets brought near. They wave off one thing and pull the other one closer.

That's right, friend. The text says they "bring near a reign of violence" (Amos 6:3). So they dismiss the day of calamity and welcome violence closer. I think that's a rough trade, and that's before we even get to the rest of the verse.

You got it, baker. Amos says, "You dine on lambs from the flock and calves from the stall" (Amos 6:4). That's the best of the flock and the best of the stall, served up while they lounge. Nobody in this scene is eating over the sink.

Those sound tasty, but they're not on this table. Amos says they dine on "lambs from the flock and calves from the stall." That's a much fancier menu than loaves and figs. I think these folks would turn their noses up at a plain loaf.

Not this time, friend. Lentils and wild greens aren't in the verse. Amos says, "You dine on lambs from the flock and calves from the stall" (Amos 6:4). That's the menu of folks who are used to being served.

That's right. Amos says, "You improvise songs on the harp like David and invent your own musical instruments" (Amos 6:5). David, Israel's great king, is the comparison. So they're making music and building brand new instruments to play it on. That's a lot of creativity, friend.

Actually, the text says they do. Amos puts it right after the harp: "…and invent your own musical instruments" (Amos 6:5). So they're not just playing like David, they're building new instruments too. I think somebody in that crowd had a very full garage.

Yes, grieve. Amos says they drink wine, anoint themselves with the finest oils, "but you fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph" (Amos 6:6). The party kept going while the ruin went ignored. That's the heart of the woe.

Good guess, but that's not the word Amos uses. He says, "…but you fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph" (Amos 6:6). The charge is that they didn't grieve. The text doesn't say anything here about prayer.
Not quite, friend. The word is grieve, not speak. Amos says, "…but you fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph" (Amos 6:6). They had plenty of time for wine and oil, but no grief for that ruin.

explanations.answer: Into exile as the first captives
explanations.explanation: Right, and it's a hard turn. Amos says, "Therefore, you will now go into exile as the first of the captives, and your feasting and lounging will come to an end" (Amos 6:7). The ones who sat first in comfort go first into exile. The ivory beds don't come along.

explanations.answer: To the palace as honored guests
explanations.explanation: That would be a nice ending, but it's not the one Amos gives. He says they "will now go into exile as the first of the captives." The feasting and lounging come to an end. I think nobody is getting a fancy invitation here.

explanations.answer: Into battle as the first soldiers
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Amos doesn't send them off as soldiers. He says they will "go into exile as the first of the captives" (Amos 6:7). Captives are the ones carried off, not the ones doing the fighting.

Yes, pride. The Lord GOD declares, "I abhor Jacob's pride and detest his citadels…" (Amos 6:8). He swore it by Himself, which is as serious as it gets. I think that fits with the folks who said they took Karnaim by their own strength.
Nope, friend. The LORD says, "I abhor Jacob's pride and detest his citadels…" (Amos 6:8). Poverty isn't what He names here. These were the comfortable ones, remember.

That's not it, friend. The LORD says He abhors Jacob's pride and detests his citadels (Amos 6:8). Weakness isn't in the verse. I think pride and weakness would be pretty hard to find at the same table.
That's right. The LORD says, "…so I will deliver up the city and everything in it" (Amos 6:8). Everything in it, friend, not just a piece. He sets that right after naming Jacob's pride and citadels.

Actually, the text says He does. The LORD declares, "…so I will deliver up the city and everything in it" (Amos 6:8). That "everything in it" is easy to skim past. It's a big sentence for a short verse.

That's right, and it's a heavy one. The relative asks, "Is anyone else with you?" and the person answers, "None" (Amos 6:10). I think this part hurts to read, so let's take it gently. It shows how complete things have become.
Not quite, friend. The person inside answers, "None" (Amos 6:10). It's a heavy verse, so no jokes here. The answer is a short word with a lot behind it.
Not this time. The one inside answers the relative's question with "None" (Amos 6:10). I think this is one of the heavier verses in the chapter. It's a short answer, and it says a lot.

Careful, this one flips it. The relative says, "Silence, for the name of the LORD must not be invoked" (Amos 6:10). So the reason is that the name must not be invoked, not that it must be called on. It's a heavy moment, and the text doesn't explain it any further.

That's right, friend. The relative retorts, "Silence," and gives this reason: "…for the name of the LORD must not be invoked" (Amos 6:10). It's the opposite of calling on the name. This is a heavy scene, so we'll let it sit.

Not so, friend. The LORD gives a command: "The great house will be smashed to pieces, and the small house to rubble" (Amos 6:11). Both houses are named, and neither one gets spared. Big or small doesn't change it.

That's right. The command covers both: "The great house will be smashed to pieces, and the small house to rubble" (Amos 6:11). The small house doesn't get a pass. It's a serious verse, and it names both sizes on purpose.

You got it. The LORD says, "But you have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood" (Amos 6:12). Wormwood is a bitter plant. Justice is meant to be the good fruit, and these folks made it taste awful.

Good try, but no. The LORD says they "turned justice into poison." Their feasts are the very thing Amos has been describing, and they hadn't turned into fasting. I think that one's a whole different sermon.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says, "But you have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood" (Amos 6:12). Wealth and ashes don't come up here. The charge is about justice and righteousness.
That's the one. They say, "Did we not take Karnaim by our own strength?" (Amos 6:13). Notice who gets the credit in that sentence. I think it's the same pride the LORD said He abhors back in verse 8.

That would be a better answer, friend, but it's not what they say. They ask, "Did we not take Karnaim by our own strength?" (Amos 6:13). The LORD isn't mentioned in their boast. They're taking all the credit themselves.
Nope. The people say, "Did we not take Karnaim by our own strength?" (Amos 6:13). No king and no plan gets named in the boast. It's all "we" and "our own."

Yes, a nation. The LORD says, "For behold, I will raise up a nation against you, O house of Israel" (Amos 6:14). It's the God of Hosts speaking, and He's talking straight to Israel. The text doesn't name that nation here.

Close, but the word is nation. The LORD declares, "I will raise up a nation against you, O house of Israel" (Amos 6:14). A king isn't named in this verse. It's a whole nation that will do the oppressing.

Not a storm, friend. The LORD says He will "raise up a nation against you, O house of Israel" (Amos 6:14). That nation will oppress them from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah. So the word you're looking for is nation.
